title: Hint & Tell: How It Works

storyboard.title: Unbox or download
storyboard.sees: A welcome screen with three fanned category cards, one line about the game, and a green privacy promise.
storyboard.does: Scans the QR on the box lid, or taps 'Play digital-only'.
storyboard.behind: The QR unlocks the box's card set offline. The app makes no account and no server call. Licensing happens later through the App Store, only if they buy the Pass.
storyboard.why: One decision only. The privacy promise sits right there, so a parent doesn't have to go looking for it.

storyboard.title: Add the family
storyboard.sees: Avatar tiles with first name and age. An 'Add' tile. A note when someone is under 18.
storyboard.does: Types first names and ages (5 people take about 60 s).
storyboard.behind: Saves the profiles in the on-device store, ready to sync to the family's own iCloud. Age decides which categories show and whether a parent has to confirm.
storyboard.why: No email and no passwords. Next time it's one tap: 'same family as last time?'

storyboard.title: Consent, person by person
storyboard.sees: Each person has a switch: 'Record my stories' or 'Play only'.
storyboard.does: Everyone chooses for themselves. A parent confirms for the under-18s.
storyboard.behind: Writes a consent record per person and per night. 'Play only' players are muted from capture: no audio is kept while it's their turn, and they can't be tagged.
storyboard.why: Consent becomes part of the game instead of fine print, and saying no costs nothing.

storyboard.title: Choose a mode
storyboard.sees: Three big cards: Classic (8 rounds), Quick (4) and Trip (3, hints only). Three switches below.
storyboard.does: Taps one card. Can flip a switch.
storyboard.behind: Sets the number of rounds, the Keeper order (fair rotation) and whether the mic pipeline loads at all. In Trip mode it never does.
storyboard.why: Every mode has the same rules; only the length changes, so nobody re-learns anything.

storyboard.title: Deal a category
storyboard.sees: The Keeper's name on top and three face-down category cards fanned out. One re-deal.
storyboard.does: The Keeper picks one card (everyone can watch).
storyboard.behind: Draws categories that fit everyone's ages and haven't come up recently. It logs nothing except the round number.
storyboard.why: Choosing from three gives a sense of control without blank-page panic. The example memories help a stuck 8-year-old.

storyboard.title: The Keeper's secret
storyboard.sees: A shielded screen: 'Only Josh look'. A field for the memory and 4 short hint fields: Where, When, Who, Object.
storyboard.does: Types the memory and 4 hints (or picks suggested hint words).
storyboard.behind: Saved locally. The on-device model can suggest hint words from the memory text using Foundation Models. Nothing goes anywhere.
storyboard.why: Hint slots have fixed labels, so kids know exactly what to write.

storyboard.title: Hints and yes/no questions
storyboard.sees: The first hint revealed, the points on offer (3→2→1) and a tracker showing '6 of 10' yes/no questions left.
storyboard.does: Players ask yes/no questions out loud. The Keeper taps YES or NO. Anyone can shout a guess.
storyboard.behind: Counts questions and reveals the next hint on a timer or a tap. No speech processing yet: this is just talking.
storyboard.why: It's 20 Questions, which everyone knows. The phone only keeps score.

storyboard.title: Guess and score
storyboard.sees: Confetti, the guesser's face, a per-player points breakdown and the scoreboard bars.
storyboard.does: The Keeper taps who guessed it (or 'nobody').
storyboard.behind: Applies the scoring rules (3/2/1, +1 Keeper) and updates the totals locally.
storyboard.why: Wrong guesses cost nothing, so shy players still have a go.

storyboard.title: Tell it
storyboard.sees: A dark 'story time' screen with a live waveform, a 2-minute ring and an 'on-device' pill.
storyboard.does: The Keeper tells the full story. Others listen (and laugh).
storyboard.behind: Mic → speech detector (SoundAnalysis) → SpeechAnalyzer transcribes on the device. The current Keeper is the speaker label. Audio and text go to the local archive.
storyboard.why: This is the heart of the night. The app does the remembering so nobody has to take notes.

storyboard.title: Everyone adds their version
storyboard.sees: A queue of faces. Tap yours to record 30 s. Reaction buttons, including 🤥 for 'contradiction'.
storyboard.does: Tap your face, speak, or skip. Tap 🤥 when versions clash.
storyboard.behind: Each tap starts a labelled clip, so the speaker is whoever tapped in. No voiceprint is needed. 'Play only' faces are greyed out.
storyboard.why: Tap-your-face labelling is honest and visible. Everyone sees what's being recorded and whose it is.

storyboard.title: Pass the phone
storyboard.sees: A big 'Pass the phone to Mum', her avatar and a hold-to-unlock bar.
storyboard.does: Hands the phone over. Mum holds the bar to open her secret screen.
storyboard.behind: Locks the next Keeper's screen behind a press-and-hold so nobody peeks. Rotation is fair: whoever has been Keeper fewest times goes next.
storyboard.why: A physical handover is the ritual. The press-and-hold stops accidental spoilers.

storyboard.title: End-of-night recap
storyboard.sees: Champion banner, stats (memories, minutes, contradictions), fun awards and a review-tomorrow toggle.
storyboard.behind: Foundation Models writes a title, a one-line summary and the 'best quote' for each memory, one memory at a time so it fits the 4,096-token context. Sync to iCloud is queued.
storyboard.why: Ends on a high, with awards for being funny or disputed as well as for winning.

storyboard.title: Morning memory review
storyboard.sees: Last night's memories as cards: title, quote, date, matched photos. Buttons to fix, hide or delete.
storyboard.does: A parent skims, fixes a name, hides one, approves the rest.
storyboard.behind: Photo matching suggests pictures by date or place. With the picker, the user chooses; with full or limited library access, it suggests. Edits sync to the family's iCloud zone.
storyboard.why: A 'human in the loop' review stops anything embarrassing from being kept by accident.

storyboard.title: On This Day nudge
storyboard.sees: A lock-screen notification: 'One week ago: The Wrong Terminal ✈️… a Who Said It round is ready.'
storyboard.behind: This is a local notification scheduled by the app itself on the phone, so no push server and no remote trigger are involved. It's per-person and easy to switch off.
storyboard.why: Brings people back with a story they care about, not a streak to protect.

storyboard.title: Who Said It round
storyboard.sees: A quote from last week ('It was the international terminal') and five faces to vote for.
storyboard.does: Everyone votes on who said it. The reveal plays the clip.
storyboard.behind: Picks quotes from consenting speakers only, using the turn labels from the earlier nights. Plays the audio from the local or iCloud archive.
storyboard.why: Past nights feed the next one, which gives a reason to keep playing.

rules_card.title: Hint & Tell: the whole game on one card
steps: Pick a card: the Keeper picks 1 of 3 categories.
Think of a memory: type it secretly, plus 4 short hints (Where, When, Who, Object).
Guess it: hints revealed one at a time; up to 10 yes/no questions between them.
Tell it: the Keeper tells the story (about 2 min); others can add their version (30 s each).
Pass the phone: the next person is Keeper. Highest score at the end wins.
safety: Veto: anyone can skip a memory, no reason needed

time_to_learn.status: design targets, to be validated in the 5-family test
rows: 'You think of a memory, we guess it'

principles.d: Every screen has one big button. Setup screens never show more than 3 choices.
The handover is part of the game. Secret screens use a hold-to-unlock so nobody spoils them.
Primary buttons are full width and about 56 pt tall, well above Apple's 44 pt minimum. Faces are 54 pt or more.
Short words, Year-3 reading level target, emoji for each category, labelled hint slots.
Questions, guesses and stories are spoken. The phone only keeps score and memory.
A waveform and 'on-device' pill while recording, and greyed-out faces for 'Play only'.

exp: Sets her own 'Record my stories' switch; Mum confirms. She feels trusted, not policed.
As Keeper she picks 'Epic Fails' and uses the labelled hint slots. She doesn't need to invent a format.
Loves the 🤥 contradiction button and the Who Said It vote. That's the social payoff.
Risk: she may not want a cringe story kept. The veto and the morning review let her hide it, no questions asked.
Never touches setup. Someone adds her as a face in 10 seconds.
When it's her turn she gets a full-screen 'Pass the phone to Nana' and one big button. Typing hints is optional: a grandchild can be her scribe.
Her story is the one the kids didn't know. The recap marks it 'New to the kids'.
Later she can join the family's shared iCloud zone via an invite link and listen, if she has an Apple Account. If not, the family can export to PDF or audio.

friction.fix: Pick from 3 categories, see example memories, fill 4 labelled hint slots
Hold-to-unlock handover; the secret screen blurs if the phone is tilted flat (design idea)

friction.f: Awkward to say no to recording
friction.fix: Per-person 'Play only' switch at setup; a default that never shames
Hint word chips suggested on-device; the Keeper can dictate hints
Audio is always kept, the transcript is editable in the morning review, and the Keeper label doesn't depend on recognition
Processing is light during play; titles and summaries are batched at the end
CKShare invite link for Apple users; PDF/audio export for everyone else

cognitive_walkthrough.method: For each of the 15 steps, ask the four standard questions: will the user try to do the right thing? Will they notice the control? Will they connect the control with their goal? Will they see progress after acting?
flags: Step 3 consent: the meaning of 'Play only' must be explicit. Copy test: 'You can still play. We just won't record you.'
Step 7: the YES/NO tap belongs to the Keeper, but others may grab the phone. Mitigation: the tracker shows 'Keeper taps'.
Step 10: if two people tap at once, take the first tap and queue the second.
Step 13: 'Hide' versus 'Delete' must be explained (hide = keep but don't show; delete = gone).

test_plan.mix: At least one family with a child aged 8–10, one with a teen, one three-generation family, one family with someone who is not confident with English, and one Android-heavy family (they play the web wedge)
test_plan.format: In the family's home, a moderated first game night of about 60 minutes. Silent observation for the first 2 rounds, then think-aloud. A 10-minute debrief. Next-morning review at home, with the morning review screen recorded only if everyone consents.
measures: Time to the first round started (target ≤ 3 min from opening the app)
Rounds completed without a facilitator stepping in
Consent choices and any second thoughts
Transcript error notes in the morning review
Would-play-again (0–10) and who asked to play again
test_plan.success: 4 of 5 families finish 4 rounds unaided and at least 3 ask to play again within a week
test_plan.ethics: Paid families, written consent covering the kids, recordings deleted after analysis, no recordings leave the family's own device

our_servers: Nothing about the family. Anonymous sales totals only, via App Store Connect

components.name: Audio capture and voice activity detection (VAD)
components.what: Turns the table's sound into speech segments, and ignores clatter.

options.pro: Built in (iOS 15+). On-device. Recognises 'speech' and 'laughter' among 300+ sounds.
options.con: Tuned for classification, not precise segmentation.

options.o: Silero VAD (open-source model via Core ML/ONNX)
options.pro: Precise speech segments. Small and cross-platform.
options.con: You bundle and maintain a model.

options.pro: Simplest and most explicit
options.con: Clunkier storytelling, and easy to forget to stop.

components.device: Any iPhone on iOS 26 (needed for SpeechAnalyzer anyway)
components.caveat: Laughter detection is a bonus signal, not something to rely on for scoring.

components.name: On-device speech-to-text
components.what: Transcribes each story so it can be searched, quoted and turned into a title.

options.pro: On-device. Model lives in system storage, not the app. Designed for long-form, distant-mic speech. en-AU in supported locales.
options.con: iOS 26+ only, and only on hardware that passes SpeechTranscriber.isAvailable. Fallback is DictationTranscriber.

options.pro: Open-source and strong accuracy. Runs on older iOS.
options.con: Large model downloads (Whisper Small is about 460 MB), heat and battery, and you manage the models.

options.pro: Wide device support
options.con: Sends audio to Apple's servers unless on-device is forced. Lower accuracy in published tests.

options.pro: Top accuracy and diarisation
options.con: DISQUALIFIED: family and children's voices would sit on a third-party server.

components.pick: SpeechAnalyzer, with DictationTranscriber as the fallback
components.device: iOS 26+. Checked at runtime via isAvailable and supportedLocales (en-AU listed).
components.caveat: All benchmarks are vendor-run tests on read speech. Kids, cross-talk, accents and a noisy dinner table will be worse. The E3 test must measure real error rates.

components.name: Speaker labelling
components.what: Knows who said what, so Who Said It works.

options.pro: No biometrics, transparent and nearly free to build. The game structure does the work.
options.con: Interjections during someone else's turn get the wrong label (fixable in review).

options.pro: Labels cross-talk automatically
options.con: Error rates are still meaningful (FluidAudio reports 15.1% DER on VoxConverse). Still needs a person to name each cluster.

options.pro: Automatic names
options.con: Voiceprints used for identification are biometric, sensitive information under the Privacy Act, so consent is needed for each person, including children.

components.caveat: Optional diarisation could later help clean up interjections, but only without enrolment and only on the device.

components.name: On-device summarising
components.what: Writes each memory's title, one-line summary, best quote, place and people tags.

options.pro: Free, offline and private. Guided generation returns structured fields.
options.con: 4,096-token context covers instructions, prompt and output combined. Apple Intelligence devices only.

options.pro: Works on every device
options.con: Bland titles; uses the Keeper's typed secret as the title.

options.pro: Better writing
options.con: DISQUALIFIED for the same reason as cloud speech

components.pick: Foundation Models, one memory per call, with a template fallback
components.device: Apple Intelligence iPhones (iPhone 15 Pro and later). Language and region must be supported, and up to about 8 GB (some models about 14 GB) free storage for Apple Intelligence.
components.caveat: A 2-minute story (about 300 words) fits comfortably. A whole night does not, so the app processes one memory at a time. Not for facts or world knowledge.

components.name: Photo matching
components.what: Suggests photos from the same day or place as the memory.

options.pro: No Photos permission needed
options.con: No automatic suggestions

options.pro: Suggestions from the photos the user chose to share
options.con: Only sees the selected set

options.o: PhotoKit full access, matching on creationDate and location
options.pro: Best 'that's the day!' moments
options.con: A big permission ask. Must be opt-in later, not at setup.

components.pick: Picker first; offer limited access from the morning review
components.caveat: Dates in memories are fuzzy ('the summer Josh was 6'), so treat matches as suggestions only.

components.name: Family sharing and sync
components.what: Shares the archive across the family's devices and with grandparents.

options.o: CloudKit private database + CKShare zone-wide share
options.pro: Data lives in the family's iCloud, never ours. Apple handles invites. Shared data counts against the owner's quota.
options.con: Participants need an Apple Account

options.pro: Reaches Android families, and the data is still in the user's own storage
options.con: A second sync engine and conflicts. There's no Android equivalent of SpeechAnalyzer plus Foundation Models: ML Kit GenAI speech is alpha, en-US, on a limited device list.

options.pro: Easy cross-platform
options.con: BREAKS the rule that private user data never touches our servers

components.caveat: Mark story fields as encrypted (CKRecord encryptedValues). Free 5 GB iCloud tiers fill up with audio, so offer compressed AAC and a 'transcript only' setting.

components.name: Licensing and payments
components.what: Sells the Family Pass. This is the only server-side touchpoint, and it's Apple's.

options.o: StoreKit 2 auto-renewing subscription with Family Sharing
options.pro: One purchase covers up to 6 family members. Apple handles receipts. We see sales totals only.
options.con: Apple's commission

options.pro: Good gift and retail story
options.con: Code fraud and redemption logic

options.o: Web checkout (Stripe) for the web wedge
options.pro: No app store needed
options.con: Must keep the payment record separate from any game data

components.pick: StoreKit Family Sharing; box QR unlocks the card set offline
components.caveat: Check the current App Store commission and AU GST handling before pricing.

components.name: Export and the box yearbook
components.what: Lets families keep their memories forever, without us.

options.pro: Portable and no lock-in
options.con: Large files

options.o: Printed yearbook via a print partner
options.pro: A physical keepsake and extra revenue
options.con: Data leaves the device. Needs explicit per-order consent and a partner with no retention.

components.pick: ZIP + PDF in v1; yearbook later as an explicit, one-off upload
components.caveat: The yearbook is the one feature that sends content out, so treat it as a separate, opt-in order.

components.name: Remote play (later)

options.pro: End-to-end encrypted, Apple-run session and messaging
options.con: Apple devices only, and an extra UX mode

options.pro: Keeps the 'one phone at the table' magic
options.con: Misses distributed families

components.caveat: The game state syncs, but recording others over a call raises extra consent questions.

why.web: Cheapest and fastest. Runs on any phone, but browser speech recognition defaults to server processing, so the web version stays no-record.
why.native: Unlocks on-device speech and summarising, CloudKit and StoreKit Family Sharing. The real product.
why.xplat: One codebase, but the iOS speech and AI APIs still need native modules, and Android on-device parity is weak (ML Kit GenAI is alpha and en-US).

explorer.note: Modelling assumption, not research: each choice shifts a rubric criterion by ±1 (bounded 1–5) from the Run 11 base scores. The totals are rubric v2.0, and the fit is the portfolio lens with monetisation fit = 3.
deltas: legal +1, pain −1, recurring −1, defend −1; privacy A
legal −1, aibuild −1; needs Chrome processLocally (experimental, en-US); privacy B
privacy C-disq → fit 0 (children's voices on a third-party server)
legal −1, aibuild −1; privacy C-redesign (biometric sensitive info)
path: Now: the paper deck (E1), under A$50
Next: the web wedge, no-record, to test the game loop (solo, under about A$1k for phases 0–2)
Then: native iOS v1. On-device speech, turn-based labels, iCloud only, digital first (A$15–40k estimate)
After E2 sales signal: the physical box
v1.x: SharePlay remote play; Android only if ML Kit GenAI leaves alpha and supports en-AU

caveats: The speech benchmarks are vendor or blog tests on read speech (LibriSpeech/FLEURS), not noisy family tables. Real accuracy must be measured in E3.
Apple Intelligence and Foundation Models need recent iPhones (15 Pro and later), with language and region limits and several GB of storage. Older phones get template titles.
Explorer scores are modelled ±1 shifts on the Run 11 rubric, not new research.
Time-to-learn figures and all UI timings are design targets.
Cost figures are Run 11 estimates (native v1 A$15–40k), not quotes.
Not legal advice: consent, the Children's Online Privacy Code, the NSW Surveillance Devices Act and biometric rules need review.
